label: EL
title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $U \in \mathcal A$ minimize $J(\cdot, F)$ in $B_1$, with $F \in L^2(B_1)$.
Then, for all $i=1,\ldots , N$,
\begin{equation}\label{EL}\Delta u^i \geq f^i \chi_{\{u^i>0\}}, \quad \Delta \hat u^i \leq \hat f_U^i, \quad \text{in $B_1,$}\end{equation} where 
$$\hat f^i_U : = f^i\chi_{\{u^i>0\}} - \sum_{j\neq i}f^j\chi_{\{u^j>0\}}+ |f^i|\chi_{\{|U|=0\}}$$
head: environment
name: Euler- Lagrange inequalities

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi \geq 0$ be a smooth function with compact support in $B_1$. 
For a given $i\in \{1,\ldots, N\},$ let $V^{\varepsilon,i}=(v^1,\ldots,v^i,\ldots v^N)$ with  
$$v^i:=(u^i - \varepsilon \varphi)^+, \quad v^j=u^j \quad \text{for } j\neq i ,$$ 
where, for  clarity of exposition,  we have suppressed the dependence of the components on $\epsilon$.
Then $V^{\varepsilon,i} \in \mathcal A$, and hence comparing $J(V^{\varepsilon,i})$ and $J(U)$ we deduce that  
$$\int_{B_1} \frac 1 2 (|\nabla (u^i-\varepsilon \varphi)|^2 -|\nabla u^i|^2) dx \geq  \int_{B_1} (f^i u^i  - f^i(u^i-\varepsilon \varphi)^+) dx.$$ After dividing by $\varepsilon,$ and restricting the integral on the right hand side on its support $\{u^i>0\},$ we get 
$$\frac 1 2 \varepsilon \int_{B_1}|\nabla \varphi|^2 dx - \int_{B_1} \nabla u^i \cdot \nabla \varphi dx \geq \int_{B_1} f^i \varphi \chi_{\{u^i>0\}} dx - \int_{B_1\cap \{0<u^i<\varepsilon \varphi\}}|f^i||\varphi| dx.$$ Here we have used that
$$(u^i-\varepsilon\varphi)^+=u^i-\varepsilon \varphi + (u^i - \varepsilon \varphi)^-,$$
and that the term $(u^i - \varepsilon \varphi)^-$ is bounded by $\varepsilon\varphi$.

Letting $\varepsilon \to 0$ the first inequality in \eqref{EL} follows.



For the second inequality, again fix  $i$ and $\varphi$ as above, we define $V^{\varepsilon,i}=(v^1, \ldots, v^N) \in \mathcal A$ such that 
$$\hat v^i= \hat u^i + \varepsilon \varphi,$$ 
that is  
$$v^i:=(\hat{u}^i + \varepsilon \varphi)^+, \quad v^j:=(u^j-\varepsilon \varphi)^+ \quad \text{for $j \neq i$}.$$






Let us notice that for any vectorial function $W \in \mathcal A$, and $i$ fixed
$$J(W)= \int_{B_1} (\frac 1 2 |\nabla \hat{w}^i|^2 +  F \cdot W)dx.$$ Therefore, comparing $J(U)$ with $J(V)$ we obtain the desired inequality  from similar computations as those above.

label: Uobar
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Uobar} If 
\begin{equation}\label{case1}
    \lim_{r\to \infty} \frac{a_r}{r^2} = \infty.\end{equation} Then, there exists a sequence of radii $r_j \to \infty$ such that
$$U_j(x):=\frac{U(r_j x)}{a_{r_j}} \to \mathcal U_0, \quad \text{uniformly on compact sets},$$ with $\mathcal U_{0}$ a non-trivial $m_0$-homogeneous minimizer to $J_0:=J(\cdot, 0)$ with $m_0 \leq m$. 




In particular, in a neighborhood of a point where  $\partial \{|\mathcal U_0| >0\}$ is smooth, 
$\partial \{|U_j| >0\}$ converges in $C^{1,\alpha}$ to $\partial \{|\mathcal U_0| >0\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Once we establish the existence of the $U_j$'s, the claim on the convergence of the free boundaries follows immediately from Propositions \ref{pert} and \ref{prop:asympt}.

Denote by $$b_{j}:=a_{2^{j}}, \quad b_j =O(2^{mj})$$ where the last inequality follows from our growth assumption.
Fix $\delta>0$ small. Then, it follows that there exists a sequence $j_k \to \infty, k\to \infty,$ such that, for every $l=0,1,\ldots, $ 
$$b_{j_k+l} \leq 2^{(m+\delta)l} b_{j_k},$$ for all large $k$'s. This is because the sets $$S_l:=\{k \in \mathbb{N} \ | \frac{b_{k+s}}{b_k} \leq 2^{s(m+\delta)}, \ s=1, \ldots, l, \}$$ are unbounded, in view of the growth of the sequence $b_j.$

Thus, the sequence $$U_{j_k}(x):=\frac{U(2^{j_k}x)}{b_{j_k}}$$
satisfies 
$$\|U_{j_k}\|_{L^\infty(B_1)} = 1, \quad |U_{j_k}(x)| \leq 2^{l(m+\delta)}, \quad \text{in $B_{2^l}$}$$ for all large $k$'s.

Moreover, as $k\to \infty$, since \eqref{case1} holds, $$F_{j_k}(x):= \frac{r^2}{a_r}F(r x) \to 0, \quad r=2^{j_k}.$$
Thus, we can extract a convergent subsequence $U_{j_k} \to \mathcal U$ uniformly on compact sets, which minimizes $J_0$ and 
$$\|\mathcal U\|_{L^\infty(B_1)} =1, \quad \mathcal U(x)= O(|x|^{m+\delta}) \quad \mbox{as $|x| \to \infty$}.$$

Now, by Almgren's frequency formula, the function
$$\gamma_{\mathcal U}(r):= \frac{r\int_{B_r}|\nabla \mathcal U|^2 dx}{\int_{\partial B_r} |\mathcal U|^2 d\sigma}$$ is increasing and in view of the growth of $\mathcal U$ we get that 

$$\bar \gamma:=\lim_{r\to \infty} \gamma_\mathcal U(r) \leq m+\delta.$$
 Here we used that 
\begin{equation}\label{gammaUderivative}
\gamma_\mathcal U(r) = \frac r 2 \frac{d}{dr} \log \fint_{\partial B_r} |\mathcal U|^2d \sigma .
\end{equation} 


We claim that there exists a non-zero homogeneous of degree $m_0:=\bar\gamma$ minimizer $\mathcal U_0$ to $J_0$ such that, 

$$V_{R}(x):=\frac{\mathcal U(R x)}{\|\mathcal U\|_{L^\infty(B_{R})}} \to\mathcal U_0, \quad \text{on compact sets along a subsequence $R=R_l\to \infty.$}$$ Notice that
$$\gamma_{V_R}(r) = \gamma_\mathcal U(Rr) \leq m_0.$$ From here, using \eqref{gammaUderivative}, we have that $L^2$ norm of $V_R$ on $\partial B_r$ is bounded in terms of $r$ and $m_0$ ($r \geq 1$).
We conclude that we can extract a convergent subsequence $V_{R_l}$ that converges uniformly on compact sets to a function $\mathcal U_0$ with
$$\gamma_{\mathcal U_0} (r) =m_0, \quad \|\mathcal U_0\|_{L^\infty(B_1)}=1.$$ Hence $\mathcal U_0$ is a non-zero homogeneous minimizer of degree $m_0.$

Therefore, given $\varepsilon>0$ we can choose $R_l$ such that  $|V_{R_l} - \mathcal U_0| <\varepsilon$ in $B_{1/\varepsilon}$ and hence the rescaling $$\frac{U(r_j x)}{a_{r_j}}, \quad r_j:=2^{j_k}R_l$$ are well-approximated by $\mathcal U_0$ in $L^\infty$, which proves the lemma with $m_0 \leq m+\delta$. Now, taking a sequence of $\delta \to 0$ and using a diagonal subsequence argument, we obtain the conclusion for an $m_0\leq m,$ as in the last part of the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
In view of the Remark \ref{U0n2},
it suffices to show that $|\mathcal U_0|:=r^{k/2}|\cos \frac k 2 \theta|$ with $k\geq 4$ cannot occur as a blow-down type I cone in the conclusion of Lemma \ref{Uobar}.





Assume by contradiction that such a $\mathcal  U_0$ is a blow-down. Then $\{|\mathcal U_0|>0\}$ consists of $k$ sectors of opening $\frac{2\pi}{k}$. Let $S_i^1, i=1, \ldots, l,$ denote the sectors where $u_0^1>0.$ Since ${\hat {u_0}}^1$ is superharmonic (see \eqref{EL}), these sectors cannot be adjacent to each other.
Given that $N=3$ and $k\geq 4$, we may assume without loss of generality that $l\geq 2$.

Let $x_i$ be the midpoint of the arc $S^1_i \cap \partial B_1, i=1,2, \ldots l.$
From the uniform convergence of $U_j$ to $\mathcal U_0$, and the $C^{1,\alpha}$ convergence of the free boundaries (see Proposition \ref{pert}), we know that $x_i \in \{u_j^1>0\}$ and $\{u_j^1>0\} \cap \partial B_1$ consists exactly of $l$ connected arcs. Since $\{u_j^1>0\}$ is connected, there is a polygonal path $P$ (with no self intersection) which joins two different $x_i$'s, fully contained in $\{u_j^1>0\}$. Moreover, by cutting off the polygonal line wherever it intersects the boundary of $B_1$, we may assume that $P$ connects two $x_i$'s (possibly different than the ones we started out with) and either lies completely inside $B_1$ or completely in $\bar B_1^c$ (except for the endpoints). 


We claim that $P$ must lie in $B_1$. Indeed, say $P$ joins $x_1, x_2$, and assume by contradiction that it lies outside $B_1$. Then $P$ and the segments from the origin to $x_1$ and $x_2$ respectively, enclose a compact region $D$. Thus, there is at least a component of $U_j$ (different than $u_j^1$), say $u_j^2,$ such that the open set 
$$\mathcal O:=\{u_j^2>0\} \cap \bar{B}^c_1 \cap D$$ is non-empty. 
Notice that the maximum of $u_j^2$ in the compact set $\overline{\mathcal O}$ has to occur in the interior, which contradicts the fact that $u_j^2$ is subharmonic ($f_2 \geq 0$).
Indeed $u^2_j=0$ on the portion of the boundary $\partial \{u_j^2>0\}\cap \partial \overline{\mathcal{O}}$, while 
uniform convergence of $U_j$ to $\mathcal U_0$ in $B_2$ shows that the maximum cannot occur on $\partial \overline{\mathcal O}\cap\partial B_1$.



In conclusion, $P$ lies in $B_1$, which means that it disconnects $B_1$ into two connected components, $D_2,D_3$. We deduce that $\{u_j^2>0\} \cap B_1$ cannot intersect both $D_2$ and $D_3$ (and similarly for $\{u_j^3>0\} \cap B_1$). Otherwise, again by connectivity, we could join points $y_2 \in D_2, y_3\in D_3$ with a polygonal path in $\{u_j^2>0\}$ which exits $B_1$ and reach a contradiction as above with the roles of $u_j^1$ and $u_j^2$ reversed. On the other hand, since $S^1_1$ and $S^1_2$ are not adjacent, $D_2$ (and $D_3$) must intersect either $\{u^2_j>0\}$ or $\{u^3_j>0\}.$


Thus, say, 
$$\{u_j^2>0\} \cap B_1 \subset D_2 \quad \text{and} \quad \{u_j^3>0\} \cap B_1 \subset D_3.$$ 
This implies that in $B_1$
$$\partial \{u_j^2>0\} \cap \partial \{u_j^3>0\} = \emptyset$$
which means that 
$$\partial \{u^2>0\} \cap \partial \{u^3>0\} \cap B_{r_j}= \emptyset$$
for a sequence of $r_j\to \infty$, contradicting our assumptions.

title: Proof
body_md:
The convergence on compact subsets of $B_1$ of the rescalings of $U$ along a subsequence is trivial. We only need to show that the limit $U_0^F$ is 2-homogeneous. Then up to a further rescaling, the claim follows.


By Caccioppoli's inequality (see Lemma \ref{lem:Caccioppoli}), we have 
$$\Phi_{U}(1/2) \leq C(\|U\|^2_{L^\infty(B_1)} + \|F\|^2_{L^\infty(B_1)}),$$ which after rescaling gives,
$$\Phi_{U}(\frac r 2) \leq C((\frac{a_r}{r^2})^2 + \|F\|^2_{L^\infty}).$$ Thus, since $\Phi_U$ is monotone, we obtain that it is bounded above and has a finite limit $\Phi_U(+\infty).$ Therefore, using that $U_{r_j}$ converges uniformly to $U_0^F$ on compact subsets of $B_1$, together with Lemma \ref{H1loc} we get
$$\Phi_{ U}(r_j\rho) = \Phi_{U_{j}}(\rho) \to \Phi_{U_0}(\rho).$$
This gives that $\Phi_{U_0^F}(\rho)= \Phi_U(+\infty)$ is constant, and $U_0^F$ must be 2-homogeneous.

title: Proof
body_md:
If \eqref{c2} holds, then the blow-up must be $U_0^F$ by the  monotonicity formula,  Proposition \ref{Weiss},  and the classification of $2$-homogeneous solutions in Section \ref{subsec:global}. 

If \eqref{c1} holds, then as in the proof of Lemma \ref{Uobar}, we end up with a type I blow-up homogeneous solution $\mathcal U_0$ of homogeneity at most $2+\delta$, for some $\delta >0$ as small as we wish. This means that either $\mathcal U_0$ is $3/2$-homogeneous as above, or it is $2$-homogeneous i.e. 
$$\mathcal U_0= c|xy|, \qquad \hbox{for some } c> 0.$$ 









We show that this last possibility cannot occur. Otherwise, there is a sequence of annuli $B_{2r_k} \setminus B_{r_k}$, $r_k \to 0$, on which $|U|>0$ consists of 4 connected components. This follows from the fact that $U_{r_j} \to \mathcal U_0$ uniformly in $B_1 \setminus B_{1/2}$ and the free boundaries $\Gamma(U_i) \to \Gamma(\mathcal U_0)$ in the $C^{1,\alpha}$ sense due to Proposition \ref{pert}.
As in the proof of Lemma \ref{time} we can infer that in a neighborhood of the origin, the set $\{|U|>0\}$ consists of precisely 4 connected components that we denote by $\Omega_i$, $1\le i \le 4$, such that $\partial \Omega_1 \cap \partial \Omega_3=\{0\}$, and $\partial \Omega_2 \cap \partial \Omega_4=\{0\}$. Then the function
$$u:=|U| \chi_{\Omega_1 \cup \Omega_3} - |U| \chi_{\Omega_2 \cup \Omega_4},$$
has Laplacian that is constant in its connected components of the positivity and negativity sets, and satisfies $u \triangle u \ge 0$. By the results in \cite{AS}, we obtain $u \in C_{loc}^{1,1}$ and we contradict \eqref{c1}. 

We give a short explanation of the result in \cite{AS} and how the $C^{1,1}$ regularity of $u$ is obtained at the origin. Since the Laplacian has a positive jump from $\{u>0\}$ to $\{u<0\}$ then the absolute value of the directional derivatives $\partial _e u$ are subharmonic (see for example Lemma \ref{impro} below). Then one can apply the ACF monotonicity formula for $(\partial_e u)^+$ and $(\partial_e u)^-$ and find that they can grow at most linearly near the origin.

label: impro
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{impro} Let $u_0 \in C^1(B_1)$ with $|\nabla u_0| \neq 0$, satisfy
$$\Delta u_0 = a^+\chi_{\{u_0>0\}} -a^- \chi_{\{u_0<0\}} \quad \text{in $B_1$},$$ with $a^\pm \in \mathbb R.$ Assume $u$ satisfies the same equation,
$$\Delta u = a^+\chi_{\{u>0\}} - a^-\chi_{\{u<0\}} \quad \text{in $B_1$},$$
and
$$|u-u_0| \leq \varepsilon \quad \text{in $B_1$}.$$ Set

We first show the following decay of the $L^\infty$ norm in an annulus $B_{2r} \setminus B_{r/4}.$

Assume $V$ satisfies \eqref{FBlinear2}-\eqref{b},	
then \begin{equation}\label{osc}

\begin{equation*}\label{oscnew}

from which the estimate claimed in the lemma follows (using only \eqref{b}).

name: Improvement of Flatness near type II cones

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by compactness. Assume the conclusion does not hold for a sequence of $t\to 0$ and a sequence of $\varepsilon \to 0.$ Then, by Lemma \ref{improgeneral} the rescaled double-valued function $$V_\varepsilon:= \frac{U - U_t}{\varepsilon}$$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $B_1 \setminus \{0\}$, to a solution $V$ of the linearized equation \eqref{FBlinear}-\eqref{transmission}, with $\|V\|_\infty \leq 1.$ We now apply Lemma \ref{tt} and conclude that  




\begin{equation} |V_\varepsilon- V_{{\bf m},p,q}|\leq \frac 1 4 \rho^2 \quad \text{in $B_{2\rho}$}\end{equation} for a polynomial $V_{{\bf m},p,q}$ with universally bounded coefficients. This implies that $U$ satisfies the conclusion of the lemma and we get a contradiction. Indeed, using that $U_t(x)$ is $C^{1,1}$ with respect to the variables $(x,t)$ in the annulus $B_{2\rho} \setminus B_{\rho/2}$, and denoting $\bar {\bf m}=-{\bf m}$,
$$\frac{\tilde{U}_{t+\varepsilon p} - U_t}{\varepsilon} = {\bf m} \cdot  \nabla U_t + q\partial_{\theta} U_t + p \partial_t(U_t) + O(\varepsilon)$$
$$= {\bf m} \cdot \nabla U_0 + q\partial_{\theta} U_0 + p \partial_t(U_t)|_{t=0} + O(\varepsilon) + O(\delta)$$
$$ = V_{{\bf m}, p,q} + O(\varepsilon) + O(\delta)$$
with the constants for $O(\varepsilon), O(\delta)$ depending on $\rho.$ In conclusion, as double-valued functions,  




$$|U -\tilde{U}_{t+\varepsilon p}| \leq \frac \varepsilon 2 \rho^2 \quad \text{in $B_{2\rho} \setminus B_{\rho/2}$}$$
hence  
$$d(U,\tilde{U}_{t+\varepsilon p}) \leq \frac \varepsilon 2 \rho^2 \quad \text{in $B_{2\rho} \setminus B_{\rho/2}$}$$
and since the distance is subharmonic (Lemma \ref{duv}), the inequality extends to  $B_{2\rho}.$
head: environment

label: begin
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\partial \{u^i>0\} \neq \emptyset$, by non-degeneracy
$$\max_{\partial B_r} u^i \geq cr^2, \quad \text{for all large $r$'s.}$$ By Proposition \ref{not1}, any type II blow-down limit of $U$ must be equal to a rotation of the 2-homogeneous solution $U_0$. By Remark \ref{all}, given $\varepsilon_1$ small to be made precise later, there exists $R=R(\varepsilon_1)$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{begin}d(U_r, U_0(e^{iq_r}x)) \leq \varepsilon_1 \quad \text{in $B_1$, for all $r\geq R.$}\end{equation}
Given a large $r$ as above, we want to apply Proposition  \ref{IF} and iterate it. First we remark that, after relabeling $\rho$, the conclusion of the Theorem holds in the ball $B_\rho(\varepsilon {\bf m})$. This means that the quadratic rescaling of $U$ from $B_{\rho r}(\varepsilon {\bf m})$ to $B_1$ is approximated by a rotation of $U_{t_1}$, with error $\varepsilon_1 \rho^\alpha$ in $B_1$, for some $|t_1|\leq C\rho^{-1} \varepsilon_1.$ If $|t_1| \leq \delta$, we can apply the Improvement of Flatness again. We do so iteratively and obtain a sequence of nested balls $B_{r_k}(z_k)$, $r_k=r \rho^k$, in which the rescaling of $U$ from these  balls to the unit ball is approximated by a rotation of $U_{t_k}$, with error $\varepsilon_1 \rho^{k\alpha}$ in $B_1$, for some $|t_k|\leq \delta.$ We stop the process when $|t_k|>\delta$. 

We prove by induction that $0 \in B_{r_{k}/2}(z_{k})$  and that the process cannot stop if $r_k \geq R.$ Indeed, if $r_k \geq R$ then, 
$U_{r_k}$ is $\varepsilon_1$ close in $B_1$ to a rotation of $U_0$ (by \eqref{begin}) and $\varepsilon_1$ close in $B_1(z_k/r_k)$ to $\tilde U_k$, that is a rotation of $U_{t_k}$ translated by $z_k/r_k \in B_{1/2}$, $|t_k| \leq \delta$. Thus, 
$$d(U_{0}(e^{iq_{r_1}}x), \tilde U_k)\leq 2\varepsilon_1 \quad \text{in $B_{1/4}$.}$$
The inequality above implies that $$|t_k|, |z_k/r_k| \leq \eta(\varepsilon_1), \quad \text{$\eta(\varepsilon_1) \to 0$ as $\varepsilon_1\to 0.$}$$
This means that $|t_{k+1}|\leq \delta$ and $|z_{k+1}/r_{k+1}| \leq 1/2$, provided $\varepsilon_1$ is chosen small depending on $\delta$ and $\rho$. 

In conclusion, in any fixed ball $B_{R'}$ with $R' \geq R$, we can approximate the rescaling $U_{R'}$ in $B_1$ by a translation and rotation of $U_t$ with arbitrarily small error $\varepsilon_1 \rho^{k\alpha}$ by starting the process above with $r=R'\rho^{-k}$. Hence, the desired conclusion follows.

\qed

title: Proof
body_md:
We divide by $t$, and then the rescaled error function 
$$V_{\varepsilon,t}=\frac{\frac 1 t U- \frac 1 t U_t}{\varepsilon},$$
by Lemma \ref{improgeneral} converges (on subsequences) as $t \to \infty$, $\varepsilon \to 0$ uniformly on compact sets of $B_1 \setminus \{0\}$ to a double-valued harmonic function $V \in \mathcal D$. By Lemma \ref{expz}, we have
$$|V-V_{{\bf m},p,q}| \le \frac 1 8 \rho^{3/2} \quad \mbox{in} \quad B_{2\rho}.$$
The conclusion follows by using that (see \eqref{36})
$$\frac 1 t U_t \to \mathcal U_0 \quad \mbox{in} \quad C^1(B_{2 \rho} \setminus B_{\rho/2}), \quad \quad t\frac {d}{dt} (\frac 1 t U_t) \to 0 \quad \mbox{uniformly in $B_{2 \rho} \setminus B_{\rho/2}$},$$ 
as $t \to \infty$, hence
\begin{align*}
\frac 1 t \tilde U_{t'}& =(1+p \varepsilon)\frac {1} {t'} \tilde U_{t'}\\
&=\frac 1 t \tilde U_t + p \varepsilon \frac {1} {t'} \tilde U_{t'} + o(1)\varepsilon\\
&= \frac 1 t U_t + \varepsilon q \partial_\theta \mathcal U_0 + \varepsilon {\bf m} \cdot \nabla \mathcal U_0 + p \varepsilon \mathcal U_0 + o(1)\varepsilon\\
&= \frac 1 t U_t+ \varepsilon V_{{\bf m},p,q} + o(1)\varepsilon,
\end{align*}
with $o(1) \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$, which gives the desired conclusion in the annular region $B_{2\rho} \setminus B_{\rho}$. This can be extended to the whole region because of the subharmonicity of $d(U, \tilde{U}_{t'}).$

title: Proof

We can iterate Proposition \ref{IF} and obtain a sequence of nested balls $B_{r_k}(z_k)$ and $t_k$ such that
$$d(U, \tilde U_{t_k}) \le \varepsilon r_k^{2+\alpha} \quad \mbox{in} \quad B_{r_k}(z_k),$$
$$r_k=\rho^k, \quad |t_{k+1}-t_k| \le C \varepsilon r_k^{\frac 12 + \alpha}, \quad |z_{k+1}-z_k| \le C \varepsilon r_k^{1+\alpha}, \quad z_0=0, \quad t_0=0,$$

The iteration of Proposition \ref{IF} stops the first time when 
\begin{equation}\label{tkrk}|t_k|r_k^{-1/2} > \delta.

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the min-max characterization as in \eqref{quotient}, we can see that $$\lambda_m^F \geq \lambda_m^0$$ and in particular (see \eqref{zeroeigen})$$\lambda^F_{2k+1} \geq\frac{2k+1}{2}.$$ The equality only holds if a linear combination of $\cos \frac{2k+1}{2} \theta$ and $\sin \frac{2k+1}{2} \theta$ vanishes where $U^F_0=0$ on the unit circle, which means that after rotation, the rays of $U_0^F$ belong to $\theta\in \{2l\pi/(2k+1), \;l=0,1,..,2k\}$. This cannot happen if $k=1$ and $F$ has two distinct components or $k=2$ (see \eqref{uofintro}). Thus, $ \lambda_3^F>\frac32$, $\lambda_5^F>\frac52$.

 We now claim that $2$ is a simple eigenvalue for our problem. Assume without loss of generality that  $U_0^F = 0$ consists of the rays $\theta \in \{0,\theta_1,\theta_2\}$ with $\theta_1 \in (\pi/2, \pi), \theta_2 \in (\pi, 3\pi/2)$ and $\theta_2-\theta_1 > \pi/2.$
Then, if $2$ is not simple, we can find an eigenfunction $g$ that vanishes on one ray of $U_0^F = 0$, say $\theta = 0$. Recall that,
\begin{equation*}\text{$g$ is periodic of period $4\pi$ and $g(\theta+2\pi) = - g(\theta)$.}\end{equation*} Therefore $g$ coincides with $\sin 2\theta$ in the interval $[\theta_2 - 2\pi, \theta_1],$ and 
$$g(\theta_1)= \sin 2\theta_1 <0, \quad g(\theta_2)= -g(\theta_2 -2\pi)=-\sin(2\theta_2 - 4\pi)<0.$$ On the interval $[\theta_1, \theta_2]$, $$g(\theta)= a \cos(2(\theta-\tau))$$ for some $a,\tau.$ Given the behavior of $g$ at $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and the fact that $\theta_2-\theta_1>\pi/2$, we deduce that $a>0$ and $\tau \in [\theta_1,\theta_2].$ Without loss of generality we can assume that $\tau \leq \pi$ and $\theta_1$ is the point of intersection of the graphs of $\sin 2\theta$ and $a \cos(2(\theta -\pi))$ and therefore belongs to the interval $(\pi/2, 3\pi/2).$ Thus, we cannot satisfy the free boundary condition \eqref{g'} since 
$$g'(\theta_1^-)<0, \quad g'(\theta_1^+)>0$$
and hence their difference is positive while $g(\theta_1)<0.$ We conclude that $2$ is a simple eigenvalue. Since $\lambda^F_m$ varies continuously with $F,$ we deduce that $\lambda_3^F$ and $\lambda_4^F$ are both simple, hence $\lambda_3^F<2.$

title: Proof
body_md:
The existence of such a function $G$ is a consequence of the fact that $|x|^{\lambda_3}g_3^F(\theta)$ solves the linearized equation. We provide the details below.

Assume as in the previous proof that $\{U_0^F=0\}$ consists of $\theta \in \{0,\theta_1, \theta_2\}.$ Let
$$u=U^F_0, \quad v= |x|^{\lambda_3}g_3^F(\theta).$$ When $\theta$ stays at distance $c_0$ away from $0, \theta_1, \theta_2$ we define 
$$G:=u+ v$$ 
which  satisfies  the desired equation with no error. In a neighborhood of a ray, say $\theta=0$, we define $G$ as a domain deformation of $u$:
$$G\left(y\right)=u(x), \quad y:=x- \frac{v}{\partial_{x_2}u}e_2.$$
We glue the two constructions using a standard partition of unity function in the $\theta$ variable, and at the end we multiply the function with a cut-off function in the radial variable to make $G$ identically zero in a large ball around the origin.


\

Let's check that  such a function satisfies the desired equation in a neighborhood of the rays at a point at distance $r>1$ from the origin. 

 After a quadratic rescaling $G(rx)/r^2$, the rescaled function $G_\varepsilon$ in $B_2 \setminus B_1$ away from the ray $\theta=0$ takes the form $$G_\varepsilon= u+ \varepsilon v, \quad \varepsilon=r^{\lambda_3-2},$$ and in a neighborhood of the ray $$G_\varepsilon\left(y\right)=u(x), \quad y:=x-\varepsilon \frac{v}{\partial_{x_2}u}e_2.$$
 


We check that in the second case
\begin{equation}\label{deltageps}\Delta G_\varepsilon(y)=\Delta u(x) + O(\varepsilon^2),\end{equation} away from $\theta=0.$
This follows from the chain rule and the fact that $\Delta u$ is constant and $v$ is harmonic on either side of the ray $\theta=0$. Notice that the change of variable $x \to y$ is of class $C^{1,1}$ across the ray since the normal derivatives of $\frac{v}{\partial_{x_2} u}$ are equal due to the free boundary condition. 

We provide some details to justify \eqref{deltageps}. Given a domain deformation
$$x \to y= x+ \varepsilon \Phi(x),$$ 
since 
$$D_y x = I - \varepsilon D\Phi + O(\varepsilon^2), \quad D^2_y x = -\varepsilon D^2 \Phi + O(\varepsilon^2),$$
we compute using the chain rule the Laplacian of $u$ with respect to $y$:
$$\Delta_y u = \Delta_x u -\varepsilon(2 u_{ij}\Phi_i^j+u_j\Phi^j_{ii}) + O(\varepsilon^2)=$$
$$= \Delta_xu -\varepsilon (\nabla u \cdot \Phi)_{ii} + \varepsilon (\Delta u)_j\Phi^j +O(\varepsilon^2).$$ This gives the equation \eqref{deltageps}.

Moreover, using that $$x= y-\varepsilon \Phi$$ and expanding $u$ around the point $y$, we get the expansion
$$G_\varepsilon(y)= u(y) + \varepsilon v(y) + O(\varepsilon^2).$$

label: impapp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{impapp} Let $U$ be a minimizer of $J(\cdot, F)$ in $B_1$, and fix $\alpha \in (0,1)$. Assume that for $\varepsilon \leq \varepsilon_0$, $\varepsilon_0$ small depending on $\alpha$ and $F$, 
$$d(U, |G_\varepsilon|)\leq \varepsilon^{1+\alpha} \quad \text{on $\partial B_1$.}$$ 
Then after a translation of $U$ by a vector of length at most $C\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}$ we have
$$d(U, |G_{\varepsilon'}|)\leq \rho^2(\varepsilon'\rho^{\lambda_3-2})^{1+\alpha} \quad \text{in $B_\rho$,}$$ with $|\varepsilon'-\varepsilon|\leq C\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}$ and $\rho$ universal.
head: environment

label: iterate
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{iterate} The conclusion in the lemma above can be iterated (after a translation of $U$) in $B_\rho$ since the quadratic rescaling $ \rho^{-2}U(\rho x)$ is approximated in $B_1$ with error $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon'\rho^{\lambda_3 -2}.$ Equivalently, we can write the statement of the lemma in an unrescaled setting in the following way. If
$$d(U, |G_t|) \leq t^{1+\alpha}r^\gamma, \quad \text{in $B_r$} \quad
tr^{\lambda_3 - 2} \leq \varepsilon_0,$$ with the relationship between $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ given by
$$\gamma=2+(\lambda_3 - 2)(1+\alpha),  \quad \gamma \in (2\lambda_3-2, \lambda_3)$$
then, 
$$d(U, |G_{t'}|) \leq t'^{1+\alpha}(\rho r)^\gamma \quad \text{in $B_{r\rho}(z)$}$$ with 
$$|t' - t| \leq C t^{1+\alpha}r^{(\lambda_3-2)\alpha}$$
and 
$$|z|\leq C t^{1+\alpha} r^{\gamma-1}.$$

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply Remark \ref{Appppp} for $U$ and $|G_\varepsilon|$. Thus,
$$\Delta d(U,|G_\varepsilon|) \geq - C(\varepsilon^2|x|^{2\lambda_3-4})\geq C\varepsilon^2\Delta(1-|x|^{2\lambda_3-2}).$$ By the maximum principle, 
$$d(U, |G_\varepsilon|) \leq \varepsilon^{1+\alpha}+ C\varepsilon^2 \leq 2\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}, \quad \text{in $B_1$}.$$ This means that for each $\delta>0$ small, $\Gamma(U) \cap (B_1\setminus B_\delta)$ is sufficiently close to $\Gamma(U_0^F)$ provided that $\varepsilon$ is small depending on $\delta.$ As before, in this annulus we identify $U$ with a double-valued function and look at the error
$$V_\varepsilon:= \frac{U-G_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}}, \quad \|V_\varepsilon\|_{L^\infty(B_1\setminus B_\delta)} \leq 2.$$ Then, for a sequence of $\varepsilon_k \to 0$, $V_{\varepsilon_k}$ converges by Lemma \ref{improgeneral} (see also Remark \ref{remlast}) to a solution of the linearized problem associated to $U_0^F$, in $B_1 \setminus B_\delta$. Here we have used that $G_\varepsilon$ solves our problem with an error $O(\varepsilon^2)$ and that $\alpha<1.$ Moreover, as $\delta \to 0$, this limit solution converges to the solution of the linearized equation in the full ball $B_1$ (see Lemma \ref{extend}). 
In conclusion, if $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small, $$V_\varepsilon = {\bf m} \cdot \nabla U_0^F + p r^{\lambda_3}g_3^F(\theta) +O(\rho^2), \quad \text{in $B_{2\rho} \setminus B_\delta$}.$$ Thus, from the definition of $V_\varepsilon$, since for $\varepsilon \to 0$, $\nabla G_\varepsilon \to \nabla U_0^F$
$$U=G_{\varepsilon'}(x+\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}{\bf m}) + O(\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}\rho^2), \quad \varepsilon'=\varepsilon+p\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}, \quad \text{in $B_{2\rho} \setminus B_\delta$}.$$ Thus, the translation $U(x-\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}m)$ is approximated by $G_{\varepsilon'}$ in $B_\rho \setminus B_\delta$ with an error $O(\varepsilon^{1+\alpha}\rho^2)$
and this can be extended from $\partial B_\rho$ to the full $B_\rho$ with the same maximum principle argument as before. We get the desired estimate by choosing $\rho$ sufficiently small, since $\lambda_3<2.$

title: Proof
body_md:
In a large ball $B_R$, let $U$ minimize $J(\cdot, F)$ with boundary data the function $G$ from Lemma \ref{G}. By applying Lemma \ref{impapp} (see Remark \ref{iterate}) we find a sequence of nested balls $$B_{r_k}(z_k), \quad r_k=R\rho^k$$ and a sequence of $t_k \in (\frac 1 2, 2)$ such that
$$d(U, |G_{t_k}|(x-z_k)) \leq t_k^{1+\alpha}r_k^\gamma \leq Cr_k^\gamma \quad \text{in $B_{r_k}(z_k)$}$$
$$|t_{k+1} - t_k| \leq C t_k^{1+\alpha}r_k^{(\lambda_3-2)\alpha}$$
and 
$$|z_{k+1}-z_k|\leq C t_k^{1+\alpha} r_k^{\gamma-1},$$ as long as
$$r_k \geq C(\varepsilon_0) \quad \text{large}.$$
Let $\bar k$ be the index for which that inequality above is satisfied for the last time, and call $\bar z:=z_{\bar k}.$ Then, from the inequalities above and the geometric behavior of the right hand sides it follows that 
$$|z_k-\bar z|\leq C r_k^{\gamma -1}, \quad \forall k\leq \bar k,$$
and
$$|t_{k}-1|\leq C r_{k}^{(\lambda_3-2)\alpha}, \quad \forall k\leq \bar k.$$ Thus,
$$d(U, |G_1|(x-\bar z)) \leq C r_k^\gamma \quad \text{in $B_{r_k}(\bar z),$}$$ as long as $k \leq \bar k.$ In conclusion 
$U_R(x):=U(x+\bar z)$ is a minimizer which is defined in $B_{R/2}$, satisfies 
$$d(U_R, |G|) \leq C r^\gamma \quad \text{in } B_{r}, R/2 \geq r\geq C(\varepsilon_0).$$ Now the conclusion follows by letting $R\to \infty$ and extracting a convergent subsequence of the $U_R$'s.

label: Uc11
title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of this proposition is identical to the proof of Proposition \ref{IF} once we show
that 
\begin{equation}\label{Uc11}\text{$U^F_t(x)$ as a function of the $(x,t)$ variables is $C^1$ in $B_1\setminus B_{\rho/2} \times [-\delta, \delta].$}\end{equation} 
This is clear when $t\neq 0$, according to formula \eqref{UFt} and the fact that $U_1^F$ is $C^{1,1}$ outside a fixed neighborhood of the origin. Thus, we only need to check the continuity of the derivatives as $t\to 0.$

After we establish \eqref{Uc11}, from the asymptotic expansion of $U_t^F$ we have
\begin{equation}\label{gradexp}\partial_t U_t^F |_{t=0}= r^{\lambda_3}g_3^F(\theta), \quad 
\nabla U_t^F(x)|_{t=0}= \nabla U_0^F(x).\end{equation}Then 
we can conclude that in the annulus $B_{2\rho} \setminus B_{\rho/2}$, $\bar {\bf m}=-{\bf m},$
$$\frac{\tilde{U}^F_{t+\varepsilon p} - U^F_t}{\varepsilon} 
= {\bf m} \cdot \nabla U^F_0 + q\partial_{\theta} U^F_0 + p \partial_t(U^F_t)|_{t=0} + o(1)$$
$$ = V_{{\bf m}, p,q} + o(1),$$
with
$$o(1) \to 0, \quad \text{as $\varepsilon,\delta \to 0,$}$$ and proceed as before.

Next, we prove \eqref{Uc11}. Let us compute 
$$\partial_t U^F_t= t^{-1} \beta (2 U_t^F - x\cdot \nabla U_t^F).$$
For notational simplicity, set 
\begin{equation}\label{uu0v}u:=U_t^F, \quad u_0:= U_0^F, \quad |x|^{\lambda_3}g_3^F(\theta)\end{equation} and, from the asymptotic expansion \eqref{asy}, \begin{equation}\label{exp1}u-u_0=tv+O(t^{1+\alpha}) \quad \text{in $B_1\setminus B_{\rho/2}$}.\end{equation} Away from a neighborhood of the rays $\{u_0=0\}$, the error $O(t^{1+\alpha})$ is harmonic hence also its derivatives are bounded by $O(t^{1+\alpha})$, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{doubleconv}\nabla u \to \nabla u_0, \quad t^{-1}\beta(2u-x\cdot\nabla u) \to v\quad \text{as $t\to 0$,}\end{equation} which establishes our claim in this region.

In a neighborhood of the rays $\{u_0=0\}$, say around $\theta=0$, we use that the two solutions $u$ and $u_0$ differ by $O(t)$, and therefore one is obtained from the other by a $C^{1,\alpha}$ domain deformation of norm bounded by $Ct$ (see the proof of Lemma \ref{impro} in Section \ref{sec:Proof-Lemma-impro}, equation  \eqref{dd},)
\begin{equation}\label{dd1}u(x)=u_0(x+t\phi_t(x)e_2), \quad \|\phi_t\|_{C^{1,\alpha}}\leq C,\end{equation}
with $C$ independent on $t$. 

Combining equation \eqref{dd1} with \eqref{uu0v} we obtain, \begin{equation}\label{phitt}\phi_t = \frac{v}{\partial_2 u_0} + O(t^\alpha),\end{equation} and since $\frac{v}{\partial_2 u_0}$ is a $C^{1,1}$ function, we deduce that the derivative of the error $O(t^\alpha)$ is of order $O(t^\sigma)$ for some $\sigma$ small.


Clearly \eqref{dd1} gives $\nabla u \to \nabla u_0$ as $t\to 0$ also in this region. To show that also the second part of \eqref{doubleconv} holds in this region, we use that $u_0$ is homogeneous of degree 2 and obtain
$$2u-x \cdot \nabla u= \frac{d}{ds}|_{s=1}s^2u(x/s)= \frac{d}{ds}|_{s=1} u_0(x+ts\phi_t(x/s)e_2)$$
$$= \partial_2u_0(x+t\phi_t) \cdot t \cdot \frac{d}{ds}|_{s=1}s \phi_t(x/s)$$
$$=  \partial_2 u_0 \cdot t \cdot (2-\lambda_3) \frac{v}{\partial_2 u_0} + O(t^{1+\sigma}),$$
where in the last equality we used that the function on the right hand side of \eqref{phitt} is homogeneous of degree $\lambda_3-1$. In conclusion
$$2u-x \cdot \nabla u=t \beta^{-1} v + O(t^{1+\sigma}),$$
which proves the second part of \eqref{doubleconv} as desired.

title: Lemma
body_md: $\Gamma(U_1^F)$ has a unique triple junction and in a neighborhood of the junction it consists of three $C^1$ curves that meet at $120^\circ$. $\Gamma(U_{-1}^F)$ does not have a triple junction point.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First we remark that the family $U_1^F$ is continuous in $F$ up to translations. Precisely, let $F_n \to F$, with $F_n, F$ constant and $F>0$. Then, up to subsequences, by Proposition \ref{IFgeneral}, $U_1^{F_n} \to W$ with $W$ a global solution for $J(\cdot, F)$ with expansion
$$W=U_0^F + |x|^{\lambda_3}g_3(\theta) + O(|x|^\gamma).$$
Thus, by the classification of global solutions, 
$$W=U_{1}^F(\cdot+{\bf m}).$$

Next, we show that the set of $F$'s in the first octant for which $\Gamma(U_1^F)$ has a triple junction is open and closed. Closedness is just a consequence of the uniform non-degeneracy (see Lemma \ref{ND}). To prove that this set is open, we notice that a triple junction point needs to have a type I blow-up profile. Indeed, if it has a type II blow-up profile, then it must coincide with a rotation of $U_0^F$. Then, since $U_1^F$ is asymptotic to the same cone $U_0^F$ at infinity, by Weiss monotonicity formula it must coincide with it. This is a contradiction hence at a triple junction $U_1^F$ has a type I blow-up profile. Since at infinity $U_1^F$ is asymptotic to $U_0^F$ we conclude that the sets $\{(u_1^i)^F>0\}$ are connected and therefore the type I blow-up profile coincides up to rotation with $\mathcal U_0=r^{3/2}\cos\frac 3 2 \theta.$ Now, by Theorem \ref{curves} and the continuity of $U_1^F$ up to translations, we conclude that our set is open and that near the triple junction (see Theorem \ref{curves}) the free boundary consists of $C^1$ curves meeting at $120^\circ$. 

The triple junction point is unique because of topological considerations. Indeed, since $\{(u^i_1)^F>0\}$ are connected, there are curves that lie inside these sets and connect the triple junction point to infinity. In particular this shows that no other triple junction point can exist.

The argument above applies also for $U_{-1}^F$, and since $F=(1,1,1)$
is not inside this set, this forces the set of $F$'s for which $U_{-1}^F$ has a triple junction to be empty.

title: Definition
body_md:
We say that $0 \in \Gamma(U)$ is a $Y$-singularity if it has a  2-dimensional blow-up. Precisely, set $a_r:=\max_{B_r} |U|,$ and either assume that for a sequence $r\to0$ 
$$\lim_{r\to0} \frac{a_r}{r^2} = +\infty$$
and (up to a rotation) $$U_r(x):= a_r^{-1} U(rx) \to \mathcal U_0 \quad \text{a type I Y-singularity}$$
or 
$$\liminf_{r\to0} \frac{a_r}{r^2} < +\infty$$
and (up to a rotation) $$U_r(x):= r^{-2} U(rx) \to U^F_0 \quad \text{a type II Y-singularity}.$$

label: improAPP
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{improAPP} Let $u_0 \in C^1(B_1)$ with $|\nabla u_0| \neq 0$, satisfy
$$\Delta u_0 = a^+\chi_{\{u_0>0\}} -a^- \chi_{\{u_0<0\}} \quad \text{in $B_1$},$$ with $a^\pm \in \mathbb R.$ If $u$ satisfies the same equation,
$$\Delta u = a^+\chi_{\{u>0\}} - a^-\chi_{\{u<0\}} \quad \text{in $B_1$},$$
and
$$|u-u_0| \leq \varepsilon \quad \text{in $B_1$}$$ then set 
$$v_\varepsilon:= \frac{u-u_0}{\varepsilon},$$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, $v_\varepsilon \to v$ uniformly on compact subsets of $B_1$ (up to a subsequence), and $v$ satisfies the transmission problem 
$$\Delta v=0 \quad \text{on $\{u_0\neq 0\}$}$$
$$v_{\nu^+} + v_{\nu^-} =\frac{a^++a^-}{|\nabla u_0|} v \quad \text{on $\{u_0=0\}$}.$$ Here $\nu^\pm$ are the unit normals to $\{u_0=0\}$ pointing to $\{u_0>0\}$ and $\{u_0<0\}$ respectively.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We notice that since $\Delta u_0$ is bounded, the function $u_0 \in C^{1,\alpha}$, for any $\alpha < 1$. Since $|\nabla u_0| \neq 0$ the level set $\Gamma_0:=\{u_0=0\}$ is a $C^{1,\alpha}$ hypersurface. Given that $|u-u_0|\leq \varepsilon$, the level set $\Gamma:=\{u=0\}$ is in an $O(\varepsilon)$- neighborhood of $\Gamma_0.$ Away from this neighborhood, clearly $v_\varepsilon$ is harmonic and bounded, therefore on any compact set away from $\Gamma_0$, up to extracting a subsequence, $v_\varepsilon \to v$ uniformly and $v$ is harmonic. It remains to prove that the convergence holds in a neighborhood of $\Gamma_0$ and that the limiting function satisfies the transmission condition on $\Gamma_0.$

For simplicity, say $0\in \Gamma_0$ and assume that $\nabla u_0(0)$ points in the $e_n$ direction. We pick a small enough ball $B_\rho$ so that $\partial_n u$ and $\partial_n u_0$ are bounded below in this ball by a fixed positive  constant. Notice that since also $u \in C^{1,\alpha}$ and $|u-u_0| \leq \varepsilon$, it follows that $|\nabla(u-u_0)|$ is sufficiently small.


Now, in $B_\rho$ we perform a hodograph transform by viewing the graphs of $u$ and $u_0$ as graphs of the function $w$ and $w_0$, respectively,  in the $x_n$-direction.  
That is, 
$$x_{n+1}= u(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad x_n=w(x_1,\ldots, x_{n-1}, u)$$
and similarly for $u_0, w_0.$ 
Then by differentiating the right hand side of this equivalence we obtain the second derivatives of $u$ in terms of the second derivatives of $w$ and conclude that 
$$\Delta u= a^{ij}(\nabla w) w_{ij}$$
and similarly for $u_0, w_0.$ Here $a^{ij}(\nabla w)$ is uniformly elliptic and since $w$ is $C^{1,\alpha}$ these coefficients are H\"older continuous. Thus, our equation takes the form
$$\mathcal L w:=a^{ij}(\nabla w) w_{ij} = a^+\chi_{\{x_n>0\}} - a^-\chi_{\{x_n<0\}},\quad \text{in $B_{c\rho}$}$$ (similarly for $w_0)$ in which the right hand side has a discontinuity along a hyperplane. From here we can conclude that $w$ is $C^{1,1}$ in $B_{c\rho/2}$ and $D^2 w$ is Hölder continuous on either side $\{x_n \geq 0\}$ and $\{x_n \leq 0\}$ up to $\{x_n=0\}$ with a discontinuity only in the $w_{nn}$ term which accounts for the discontinuity of the right hand side (see Remark \ref{rem85} below).



Now we look at 
$$\phi_\varepsilon:=\frac{w-w_0}{\varepsilon}$$
which solves the equation 
\begin{equation}\label{phieps}
    \tilde{a}^{ij}(x)(\phi_\varepsilon)_{ij} + \tilde{b}(x)\cdot \nabla\phi_\varepsilon=0\end{equation}
with $$\tilde{a}^{ij}(x):=a^{ij}(\nabla w_0) \in C^{0,\alpha}$$
and  
$$ \tilde b(x):=\int_0^1 \nabla_p a^{ij}(t\nabla w + (1-t)\nabla w_0)w_{ij} dt \in L^\infty.$$
In particular, this equation has $C^{1,\alpha}$ estimates (for all $\alpha<1$) and we get that $$\|\phi_\varepsilon\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(B_{c\rho/2})} \leq C \|\phi_\varepsilon\|_\infty \leq C.$$

In conclusion, the function $u$ is obtained from $u_0$ by the domain deformation 
\begin{equation}\label{dd}
    u_0(x)=u(x+\varepsilon \phi_\varepsilon e_n),\end{equation}
with $\phi_\varepsilon$ a function with bounded $C^{1,\alpha}$-norm. Here the pullback is still denoted by $\phi_\varepsilon$.
Therefore, \begin{equation}\label{veps}v_\varepsilon(x) = -(\partial_n u(x)) \phi_\varepsilon(x) + O(\varepsilon),\end{equation}
which, as $\varepsilon \to 0,$ proves the convergence of $v_\varepsilon$ in a neighborhood of $\Gamma_0$ to a function $$v=-(\partial_n u_0) \phi$$ which is harmonic away from $\Gamma_0.$ Now it is easy to check that the transmission condition is satisfied. To this end, since $\phi $ is $C^1$, 
it suffices to show that $\partial_n u_0$ satisfies the condition. In fact, we show that every directional derivative of $u_0$ satisfies the condition, and it suffices to show it at the origin where $\nu^+=e_n$ and $\nu^-=-e_n$. 
Let ${\bf e}$ be a unit direction. Given that the only second derivative with a discontinuity at the origin is $(u_0)_{nn}$ we have that
$$(u_0)_{{\bf e}\nu^+} + (u_0)_{{\bf e}\nu^-}= ({\bf e} \cdot e_n)((u_0)_{\nu^+\nu^+} - (u_0)_{\nu^-\nu^-})$$
$$=({\bf e}\cdot e_n)(a^++a^-)= \frac{(u_0)_{{\bf e}}}{|\nabla u_0|}(a^++a^-).$$

body_md:

$$a^{ij}(x)u_{ij}=f(x) \quad \mbox{in $B_1$,} \quad a^{ij} \in C^\alpha(B_1), \, \, f \in C^\alpha(\overline B_1^-) \cap C^{\alpha}(B_1^+).$$

label: ACF
title: Proposition

label: BoundedLaplace
title: Proof
body_md:
We divide the proof in two steps. Notice that since $F \in L^\infty$ then, after dividing by a large constant we may assume that
$$\|F\|_{L^\infty} \le 1, \quad \|U\|_{L^2} \le 1.$$
 From the Euler-Lagrange equation we get
\begin{equation}\label{BoundedLaplace}
\Delta u^i \geq -1, \quad \Delta \hat u^i \leq 1, \quad \text{in $B_1$.}
\end{equation} 

{\it Step 1.} $u^i$ is continuous and $\{u^i>0\}$ is open. In particular, from \eqref{BoundedLaplace}
\begin{equation}\label{Bpositive}|\Delta u^i| \leq 1 \quad \text{in $B_1 \cap \{u^i>0\}$}\end{equation}
which implies that $u^i \in C^{1,\alpha}$ for all $0<\alpha<1$ in its positivity set.


\smallskip

From the first equation in \eqref{BoundedLaplace} we deduce that $u^i$ plus a quadratic polynomial is subharmonic hence 
\begin{equation}\label{BoundedLaplace2}
0 \le u^i \leq C \quad \text{in $B_{3/4}$,} 
\end{equation} for a dimensional constant $C>0.$ Moreover, $u^i$ can be defined pointwise as
$$u^i(x)=\lim_{r\to 0} \fint_{B_r(x)} u^i.$$
and it is upper semicontinuous. Notice that the limit is finite since $u^i \ge 0$. Consequently, $\hat u^i$ is defined pointwise and it satisfies
$$\hat u^i(x)=\lim_{r\to 0} \fint_{B_r(x)} \hat u^i.$$ Since, $\hat u^i$ satisfies the second equation in \eqref{BoundedLaplace} we deduce from this last identity that $\hat u^i$ is lower semicontinuous. On the other hand, $u^i=(\hat u^i)^+$ which implies that it is lower semicontinuous as well. We finally conclude that $u^i$ is continuous.



{\it Step 2.} $u^i$ is Lipschitz continuous.

We assume without loss of generality that $n\geq 3$, otherwise we extend the functions trivially in one extra dimension. If $u^i(0)=0,$ then, we deduce from \eqref{BoundedLaplace} that for all $0 < r \leq 1/2,$
\begin{equation}\label{Bounds}
\frac{c}{r^2}  \fint_{B_{r}}(u^i)^2 dx + O(1) \leq \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{B_r}\frac{|\nabla u^i|^2}{|x|^{n-2}} dx \leq \frac{C}{r^2} \fint_{B_{2r}}(u^i)^2 dx + O(1).
\end{equation}
Indeed, in view of \eqref{Bpositive}-\eqref{BoundedLaplace2}, on the set $\{u^i>0\}$
\begin{equation}\label{equivalent} \frac 1 2 \Delta ((u^i)^2) = |\nabla u^i|^2+ u^i \Delta u^i =  |\nabla u^i|^2+O(1),\end{equation}
in the sense of distributions. On the other hand, $\Delta ((u^i)^2)$ as a distribution in $B_1$ is supported on $\{u^i>0\}.$ This can be seen by approximation. We write the identity above with $u^i$ replaced by the truncation $(u^i-\varepsilon)^+$, which is Lipschitz in view of \eqref{Bpositive}, then pass to the limit for $\varepsilon \to 0.$



Now, denote by  $\Gamma_\rho \in C^{1,1}$ the smoothing of the fundamental solution $\Gamma(x):=|x|^{2-n}$ which coincides with it outside $B_\rho$, and is the appropriate quadratic polynomial on $B_\rho$. Then,
$$\Delta \Gamma_\rho = c(n) \frac{\chi_{B_\rho}}{|B_\rho|},$$
$$\Gamma_\rho - \Gamma_r \leq \Gamma, \quad \rho < r,$$ and $\Gamma_\rho - \Gamma_r$ is supported in $\overline{B_r}$.
Using the latter inequality and \eqref{equivalent} to estimate $\frac{1}{r^2} \int_{B_r}\frac{|\nabla u^i|^2}{|x|^{n-2}} dx$ then passing to the limit as $\rho \to 0$, we obtain the lower bound in \eqref{Bounds}.


For the upper bound, we cut off $|x|^{2-n}$ in the annulus $B_{2r} \setminus B_r$,
use \eqref{equivalent}, and integrate by parts.



Now, let $0 \in \partial\{|U|>0\}$, so that \eqref{Bounds} holds for all $i$'s. Then applying Proposition \ref{ACF} to any pair $u^i, u^j$ we conclude that for all $k \in \{1,\ldots, N\}$, except at most one, say $k=1$,
$$\frac{1}{r^2} \int_{B_r}\frac{|\nabla u^k|^2}{|x|^{n-2}} dx \leq C, \quad k \geq 2, \quad 0<r \leq 1/4.$$ Notice that to bound the right hand side of \eqref{ACF1}, we used the bound in \eqref{Bounds} for $r=1/4.$


From the lower  bound in \eqref{Bounds} we deduce that (for a $C>0$ changing from line to line)
\begin{equation}\label{average}\frac{1}{r^2}\fint_{B_{r}}(u^k)^2 dx \leq C, \quad k\geq 2, \quad 0<r\leq 1/4.\end{equation}
Call, $$v^k(x):= \frac{u^k(rx)}{r}, \quad x\in B_{1}.$$
Then, from \eqref{BoundedLaplace} and \eqref{average} we have in $B_{1}$
$$\Delta v^k \geq - Cr, \quad \int_{B_{1}} (v^k)^2 dx \leq C,$$
therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{k2}v^k(x) \leq C \quad \text{in $B_{1/2}$, for all $k\geq 2.$}\end{equation}
We prove now that the inequality above also holds for $v^1.$ Indeed, from \eqref{BoundedLaplace} we have that
$$\Delta \hat{v}^1 \leq r \leq 1$$
and $$\hat{v}^1(0)=0.$$
 Then, by the mean value inequality for $\hat v^1$ we have
 $$C + \hat v^1(0) \geq \fint_{B_{1/2}} \hat{v}^1 dx = \fint_{B_{1/2}} (v^1 - \sum_{j \geq 2} v^j)dx$$
 and it follows from \eqref{k2} that
 $$\fint_{B_{1/2}} v^1 dx \leq C.$$ Since $v^1$ is positive and $v^1+C|x|^2$ is subharmonic, we deduce that $v^1 \leq C$ in $B_{1/4}.$ 


 In conclusion $$u^k \leq C r, \quad \text{in $B_{r/4}$, for all $k\geq 1$,}$$ which by interior regularity proves the Lipschitz continuity.

label: general
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{general} Let $0 \leq u \leq 1$ be a continuous function satisfying 
$$\Delta u \geq -1 \quad \text{in $B_1$}$$ and 
$$\{u>0\} \cap B_1 \subset\{|x_n| \leq \varepsilon\}$$
for some $\varepsilon>0$ small. Then,
$$ u \leq \varepsilon^2 \quad \text{in $B_{1/2}$}.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the maximum principle, 
$$u \leq w+\frac 12 (\varepsilon^2 -x_n^2)^+\quad \text{in $B_1$}$$
where $w$ is the harmonic function in the strip $B_1\cap \{|x_n| <\varepsilon\}$ which is zero on $\{|x_n|=\varepsilon\} \cap B_1$ and 1 on the remaining part of the boundary, and is extended to zero outside the strip $\{|x_n| <\varepsilon\}$. By Harnack inequality, 
$$\|w\|_{L^\infty(B_{1-k\varepsilon})} \leq e^{-ck}.$$ In particular, $$w \leq e^{-c/\varepsilon} \quad \text{in $B_{1/2}$},$$ and our claim follows.

label: pos
title: Proof
body_md:
From assumption \eqref{flatnew}, after relabeling the indices, we can assume that
$$\{u^i>0\} \subset \{|x_n| \leq \varepsilon\}, \quad \text{for all $i\geq 3$,}$$ and 
\begin{equation}\label{pos}u^1>0 \quad \text{on $\{x_n>\varepsilon\}.$}\end{equation}
Thus, Lemma \ref{general} implies that
$$ u^i \leq \varepsilon^2 \quad \text{in $B_{1/2}$, for all $i\geq 3$}.$$ In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{e2}|\hat u^1 - (-\hat u^2)| \leq 2 \sum_{i\geq 3} u^i \leq 2\varepsilon^2 \quad \text{in $B_{1/2}$.}\end{equation}
Moreover, from the Euler Lagrange equation,
$$\Delta \hat u^1 \leq \|F\|_\infty, \quad \Delta (-\hat u^2) \geq - \|F\|_\infty, \quad \text{in $B_1$}.$$
Let $h$ be the harmonic replacement of $\hat u^1$ in $B_{1/2}$. By the maximum principle we get that in $B_{1/2}$
$$\hat u^1 \geq h - \|F\|_\infty,$$
and by \eqref{e2}, $(-\hat u^2) -2\varepsilon^2 \leq \hat u^1=h$ on $\partial B_{1/2}$ hence
$$(-\hat u^2) -2\varepsilon^2 \leq h+\|F\|_\infty.$$



Therefore, again by \eqref{e2},
\begin{equation}\label{u1h}|\hat u^1 - h| \leq 4\varepsilon^2 + \|F\|_\infty, \quad \text{in $B_{1/2}$}. \end{equation}
From \eqref{mu0}, \eqref{flatnew}, \eqref{pos}, and Hopf Lemma, we conclude that
$$u^1 \geq c(\mu)(x_n-\varepsilon)^+.$$


Since $h$ is $2\varepsilon$ close to $\hat u^1$ we can conclude that
$$|\nabla h(0)| \geq \frac 1 2 c(\mu).$$
Using that $h$ is well approximated by its linear part, and by choosing $\varepsilon$ small enough, we get that after a homogeneous of degree one rescaling from $B_{r_0}$ to $B_1$ and multiplication by a constant, we may assume that
\begin{equation}\label{flat} |U-(x_1^+, x_1^-, 0,\ldots, 0)|\leq \varepsilon_0, \quad \text{in $B_1,$}\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{smallF} \|F\|_\infty \leq \delta\varepsilon_0,\end{equation}
for $r_0$ small depending on $\mu$ and $\delta, \varepsilon_0$ universal.


\

Now the argument that led to \eqref{u1h} can be iterated indefinitely in a $C^{1,\alpha}$ fashion to obtain (for a similar argument see for example \cite{DFS}),
$$|U-a_k((x\cdot \nu_k)^+, (x \cdot \nu_k)^-, 0,\ldots, 0)|\leq \varepsilon_0r^{1+\alpha}\quad \text{in $B_r$, $r=\rho^k$}$$ and $\rho$ universal, with
$$|a_{k+1}-a_k| \leq C\varepsilon_0r^\alpha, \quad |\nu_{k+1}-\nu_k|\leq C\varepsilon_0 r^{\alpha}.$$
\qed

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $V$ be an admissible competitor with $V=U$ in $B_1 \setminus \bar B_{1-\delta}$ for $\delta>0$ small. 
We use Lemma \ref{uv} below, and call $W_k$ the interpolation of $U_k$ and $V$ such that 
$$W_k= V \quad \text{in $B_{1-\delta}$}, \quad W_k=U_k \quad \text{in $B_1 \setminus \bar B_{1-\delta/2}$}.$$
Then, by the minimality of $U_k$ and Lemma \ref{uv}, we get
$$J_k(U_k, B_1) \leq J_k(W_k, B_1) \leq J_k(V, B_{r_k}) + J_k(U_k, B_1 \setminus \bar B_{r_k}) + o(1),$$
with $o(1) \to 0$ as $k\to \infty.$ Notice that, by Caccioppoli's inequality $\|U_k\|_{H^1}$, is uniformly bounded in $B_{1-\delta/2}$ and the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{uv} apply.

We deduce that,
$$J_k(U_k, B_{r_k}) \leq  J_k(V,  B_{r_k}) + o(1).$$
By the lower semi-continuity of $J$, since $F_k \to F$ in $L^2$, we obtain that,
$$J(U, B_{\bar r}) \leq  J(V, B_{\bar r}), \quad 1-\delta \leq \bar r \leq 1-\delta/2.$$ Our claim follows by letting $\delta \to 0.$

label: uv
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{uv} Let $U_k,V_k$ be sequences in $\mathcal A$ and $\delta>0$ small. Assume that $U_k-V_k \to 0$ in $L^2(B_{1-\delta/2} \setminus \bar B_{1-\delta}),$ as $k\to \infty,$ and that $\|U_k\|_{H^1}, \|V_k\|_{H^1}$ and $\|F_k\|_{L^2}$ are uniformly bounded in $B_{1-\delta/2}$. Then, there exists $W_k \in \mathcal{A}$ with 
$$W_k:= \begin{cases}V_k \quad \text{in $B_{1-\delta}$}\\ U_k \quad \text{in $B_1 \setminus \bar B_{1-\delta/2}$}\end{cases}$$ such that, 

$$J_k(W_k, B_1) \leq J_k(V_k, B_{r_k}) + J_k(U_k, B_1 \setminus \bar B_{r_k}) + o(1),$$ 
for some $1-\delta \leq r_k \leq 1- \delta/2$,
 with $o(1) \to 0$ as $k \to \infty.$

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we prove our claim in the case when in the annular region where we interpolate we have $V_k \leq U_k,$ that is the inequality holds for each component. For notational simplicity, in what follows we drop the subscript $k$. 

Let  $\varphi(s)$ be a smooth function on $\mathbb R$, which is $0$ on $(-\infty, 0]$ and $1$ on $[1,+\infty)$ and 
for $0< \mu< \frac{\delta}{4}$, set 
$$\varphi_\mu(s) = \varphi\left(\frac{s}{\mu}\right).$$
For all $r \in [1-\delta, 1-\frac 3 4 \delta]$, denote by $\varphi_r(x):=\varphi_\mu(|x|-r)$ and define 

\begin{equation}\label{w_r}
W_r:= \varphi_r U + (1-\varphi_r)V.
\end{equation} 
Since we are assuming that $V \leq U$, this guarantees that $W_r \in \mathcal A.$
Then,
\begin{align*}J(W_r, B_1) \leq &J(V, B_r) + J(U, B_1 \setminus \bar B_{r+\mu}) + \\
\ & C\int_{B_{r+\mu} \setminus \bar B_r} (|\nabla \varphi_r|^2|V-U|^2 + \varphi_r^2|\nabla U|^2+(1-\varphi_r)^2|\nabla V|^2)dx\\  + & \int_{B_{r+\mu} \setminus \bar B_r} (\varphi_r F\cdot U+ (1-\varphi_r)F\cdot V) dx.
\end{align*}
Thus (for $C$ changing from line to line),
\begin{align*}J(W_r, B_1) \leq &J(V, B_{r}) + J(U, B_1 \setminus \bar B_{r}) + CE(r)\end{align*}
with 
$$E(r):=\int_{B_{r+\mu} \setminus \bar B_r} (\frac{1}{\mu^2}|U-V|^2 + |\nabla U|^2+|\nabla V|^2 +|F||U|+|F||V|) dx$$

We now average in $E(r)$ on the interval $[1-\delta, 1-\frac 3 4 \delta]$ and use Fubini to get 
\begin{align*} \frac 4 \delta \int_{1-\delta}^{1-\frac 3  4 \delta} E(r) dr & \leq  \frac 4  \delta \mu \int_{B_{1-\delta/2} \setminus \bar B_{1-\delta}} (\frac{1}{\mu^2}|U-V|^2 + |\nabla U|^2+|\nabla V|^2 +|F||U|+|F||V|) dx.
\end{align*}
By choosing first $\mu$ small and then $k$ large, we obtain the desired statement in view of the assumption that $\|U_k-V_k\|_{L^2} \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$.

This proves the result when $V_k \leq U_k$. Otherwise, we do this procedure twice. First we interpolate $U_k$ and $\min\{U_k, V_k\}$ between $B_{1-\delta}$ and $B_{1-3\delta/4}$, and then we interpolate the $\min\{U_k,V_k\}$ and $V_k$ between $B_{1-7\delta/8}$ and $B_{1-\delta/2}.$

title: Proof
body_md:
By compactness and optimal regularity, $U$ is Lipschitz continuous in $B_1$ and by the Euler-Lagrange equation $U \in C^{1,\alpha}(\{|U|>0\})$. The convergence is then obvious in the set $\{|U|>0\}.$


Let $x_0$ be a point where $|U(x_0)|=0$ and $U$ and all the $U_k$'s are differentiable. It suffices to show that $\nabla U_k(x_0) \to \nabla U (x_0)$, which implies the almost everywhere pointwise convergence of the gradients. 

Since $U\geq 0$, $\nabla U(x_0) = 0$. Hence, 
$$|U(x)| \leq \delta r, \quad \text{in $B_r(x_0)$, for all small $r$'s.}$$ Therefore, for a fixed small $r$ and for all large $k$'s,
$$|U_k(x)| \leq 2\delta r, \quad \text{in $B_r(x_0)$.}$$
By the optimal regularity estimate \eqref{opt} in $B_r(x_0)$,
$$\|\nabla U_k\|_{L^\infty(B_{r/2}(x_0))} \leq C(\frac 1 r \|U_k\|_{L^\infty(B_r(x_0))} + r\|F_k\|_{L^\infty(B_r(x_0))})$$
which combined with the inequality above gives, 
$$\|\nabla U_k\|_{L^\infty(B_{r/2}(x_0))} \leq C(3\delta + r\|F\|_{L^\infty(B_r(x_0))}) \leq \varepsilon$$
by choosing first $\delta$ and then $r.$

label: mu
title: Proof
body_md:
As in the proof of Lemma \ref{H1loc}, the rescaled Lipschitz estimate, gives that if
$$\liminf_{r\to 0} \frac{\|U\|_{L^\infty(B_r)}}{r}=0$$ then the first alternative holds. Otherwise, there exists $\mu>0$ such that for all small $r$'s, \begin{equation}\label{mu}\mu r \leq \|U\|_{L^\infty(B_r)} \leq \mu^{-1} r.\end{equation} Then, by compactness, the Lipschitz rescalings
$$U_r(x) := \frac{U(rx)}{r}$$ converge uniformly on compact sets to a global solution $U_0$ of $J_0,$  which satisfies \eqref{mu} as well for all $r$'s. By Almgren's frequency formula (Proposition \ref{almgren}) $U_0$ must be homogeneous of degree 1. Thus, the ACF monotonicity formula (Proposition \ref{ACF}) implies that $U_0$ must have either only one non-trivial component or two components given by $a_\pm(x\cdot \nu)^\pm.$ The former is not possible because that component, say $u^1_0$, would coincide with $\hat u_0^1$ and be superharmonic by the Euler Lagrange equation. However, it would be zero at the origin contradicting the maximum principle. Then, $U_0$ must have two components as above, and we end up in the assumptions of Proposition \ref{pert}.
